title: Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning
claim: Standard prioritization leaves distant states blocked after a local shift; adding graph-topology potentials gives them nonzero priority before updates arrive.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, same gridworld, heatmap color contrast
description: Three side-by-side copies of a four-rooms gridworld with dark walls and narrow doorways. Panel (a), 'Local reward shift', shows a blank grid with an orange star in the upper-right room, surrounded by a faint orange glow, and the note that the initial residual is positive. Panel (b), 'Standard PS after K=4 backups', shows purple shading limited to the starred room and a single doorway cell. Gray crosses mark every other cell as blocked with zero priority, and an arrow labelled 'reactive predecessor wavefront' points toward the doorway. Panel (c), 'GTA-PS topology priority', fills the whole grid with a teal-to-dark-blue gradient, darkest near the star, and includes the formula tau = gamma(I - gamma P)^-1 xi. Arrows point toward the star, and the caption says priority is dense before the wave arrives. The eye goes first to the star, then to the contrast between the gray crosses in (b) and the full color in (c).
caption: A localized reward shift creates sparse residual at $s_r$. Standard PS is shortsighted: priority of distant states receives no information hints. Spectral Prioritized Sweeping (SPS / GTA-PS) adds a topology potential on the policy-induced graph, assigning nonzero topology scores to upstream states before predecessor pushes reach them.
abstract: Prioritized Sweeping (PS) accelerates model-based reinforcement learning by selecting backups according to residual magnitude. In nonstationary reward settings, however, the canonical priority score is shortsighted. After a localized reward shift, residuals propagate only through realized backups; so clogged or distant state estimates may become idle under a limited replanning budget. We introduce Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS), a concrete instance of our general topology-guided principle for controlled planning. GTA-PS augments the residual key with a mixing of regularized directed-Laplacian potentials that diffuses residual information through bidirectional graph structure. The topology weight is controlled by a scheduler based on the Second Largest Eigenvalue Modulus (SLEM), allowing the order to adapt to the chain's mixing regime. We prove that the forward potential coincides with discounted residual propagation at a canonical regularization parameter, and show that GTA-PS gives nonzero priority to states that standard PS can leave blocked after sparse reward shifts. Tabular experiments on FourRooms and GARNET demonstrate improved replanning efficiency over vanilla PS under both DP and Dyna-style host planners.
